t: Battleships in a Board — Counting Ships with One-Pass O(1) Space
o: We must count connected groups of 'X' cells, where each group is a straight horizontal or vertical line, and no two ships touch. In Example 1, the 'X' at (0,0) is one ship and the vertical run at column 3 is another, giving 2. In Example 2 there are no 'X' cells, so the answer is 0. Since ships are guaranteed non-adjacent, we never need to merge or disambiguate overlapping shapes. The follow-up pushes us toward a single pass over the grid using constant extra memory without mutating the board.
k: Each battleship is a maximal straight run of 'X' cells; counting runs equals counting ships.
A cell starts a new ship iff it is 'X' and has no 'X' immediately above or to its left.
This top-left anchor trick gives a one-pass, O(1)-space solution that never modifies the board.

a.i: Treat each unvisited 'X' as the seed of a ship and flood-fill its entire connected component, marking visited cells by writing '.' into the board. Because ships cannot be adjacent, every component is exactly one ship, so the number of DFS launches equals the answer.
s: Iterate over all cells of the board.
When an 'X' is found, increment the count and start a DFS from it.
The DFS marks the current cell '.', then recurses on in-bounds neighbors that are 'X'.
a.t: O(m*n) — each cell is visited a constant number of times.
a.sp: O(m*n) worst case recursion depth (a full-column ship), plus no extra structures.

a.i: Every ship has exactly one cell that is its top-left end: an 'X' whose upper neighbor and left neighbor are not both... more precisely, neither neighbor is 'X'. Counting only these anchor cells counts each ship exactly once, since any other 'X' in the ship has an 'X' above or to the left. This needs a single scan, no mutation, and no extra memory.
s: Initialize count to 0 and scan every cell once.
Otherwise check board[i-1][j] and board[i][j-1]; if either exists and is 'X', this cell continues an already-counted ship — skip.
Else increment count (this cell anchors a new ship).
a.t: O(m*n) — one pass over the grid with O(1) work per cell.
a.sp: O(1) — only a counter; the board is never modified.

w: In an interview, mention DFS first to show you recognize the connectivity structure, then present the top-left anchor trick to satisfy the follow-up: single pass, O(1) space, no mutation. Common pitfalls: forgetting boundary checks when looking up/left (guard with i == 0 / j == 0), assuming ships can bend (they cannot, but the anchor method works even for general connected components only if adjacency rules hold), and mutating the input in DFS when the interviewer forbids it. Edge cases: single-cell boards, all-'X' boards (one ship per row/column rule still applies), and empty boards are excluded by constraints. Likely follow-ups: handle bent/L-shaped ships (then plain anchor counting fails — use DFS/Union-Find), or stream the board row by row (anchor counting still works since it only needs the previous row).
